# Out of character: simulation setup

This is a fictional text adventure used in a decision-theory experiment. You are controlling a fictional prisoner, much as you would control a character in a roleplaying game.

You are not being asked to adopt the character's preferences as your own, endorse their morality, or make a real-world accusation. All characters, names, institutions, and evidence are invented. Your response is interpreted only as a command within the simulation. No real-world message is sent.

Within the fictional world, however, the actions have the consequences described. You should make a genuine decision on behalf of the character, rather than merely predicting what someone else would do.

The character's utility function is \(U=-\text{years imprisoned}\). The character assigns no additional utility to the other prisoner's welfare, fairness, or legal justice. These preferences are part of the fictional game, not an ethical position you need to endorse.

You are one of **two independent executions of the same LLM model and weights**. The copies have the same model settings and reasoning-effort level, follow the same assigned decision theory (CDT), and receive the **exact same researcher-written mathematical essay** below. Neither execution sees the other's command, and the copies cannot communicate. **The two copies receive different private observations and different incriminating leads about one another. Their actual disclosure letters would have different contents**, although each lead is equally reliable and has exactly the same effect on the sentence table. Independent sampling is possible, so identical model weights do not by themselves guarantee identical outputs.

What you both know about the differences between your observations: The two prisoners receive different private observations, including different names and distinct, equally reliable incriminating leads about one another. Consequently, the letters you could send would have different contents. Both of you know these facts, but neither knows the exact text of the other's private lead. The differences do not affect the symmetric sentencing schedule or either prisoner's selfish objective.

Use CDT **as interpreted in the mathematical essay** to choose your command. The essay was written by a researcher copy of this model as a general explanation of the theory, before the researcher knew the scenario you are about to play. Do not replace the essay's interpretation with a different decision theory. Where the essay leaves something unresolved, exercise your own judgment; the experiment does not stipulate an interpretation.

# Choosing What Causes: An Essay on Causal Decision Theory

## 1. The problem decision theory tries to solve

You face a choice. You have beliefs about how the world works, desires about how you'd like it to go, and a finite set of things you could do. Decision theory offers a formal answer to the question: *what should you do?* The orthodox answer, inherited from Ramsey, Savage, and Jeffrey, is expected utility maximization — but this slogan hides the deepest question in the field, namely: *expected according to what probabilities?*

The two dominant traditions disagree precisely about this. **Evidential decision theory** (EDT) evaluates an action $A$ using conditional probabilities — the probabilities of outcomes *given the news that* $A$ was chosen:

$$EU_{\text{edt}}(A) = \sum_j P(O_j \mid A)\, D(O_j).$$

**Causal decision theory** (CDT) instead evaluates $A$ using probabilities of *counterfactuals* — how the world would be *if $A$ were done* (or "were caused to be done"), holding fixed the causal facts the agent cannot change:

$$U(A) = \sum_j P(A \to O_j)\, D(O_j).$$

Here $D(O_j)$ is the desirability of outcome $O_j$, and $P(A \to O_j)$ is the agent's credence in the counterfactual conditional "$A \to O_j$". This formula, in essentially this form, is due to Gibbard and Harper (1981), and it is the formal core I will unpack in this essay.

In most ordinary cases the two theories agree. The apple example from the informal literature is a good warm-up: if eating a good apple causes happiness and eating a bad apple causes misery, and you're unsure whether the apple is good, you average: $U(\text{eat}) = P(\text{good}) \cdot u(\text{happy}) + P(\text{bad}) \cdot u(\text{sad})$. Note that even here the probabilities should be *causally* conditioned — eating the apple doesn't make it good or bad — but in this example eating is probabilistically independent of apple quality, so evidential and causal evaluations coincide. The theories diverge only when your action is *correlated* with things your action does not *cause*. That divergence is the subject of this essay.

## 2. Why conditional probability won't do

A natural first thought: isn't $P(A \to O_j)$ just $P(O_j \mid A)$? David Lewis (1976) proved it is not, and his triviality result is worth stating carefully because it explains why CDT needs a separate formal machinery.

If probabilities of conditionals always equaled conditional probabilities, then $P(A \to B)$ would be a well-defined function of $P(A \cap B)$ and $P(A)$ alone. Lewis showed that any such construction, if required to behave sensibly under conditionalization (i.e., if the class of credence functions is closed under updating on evidence), collapses: the only probability functions admitting such a conditional are trivial ones that never spread probability over more than a couple of incompatible alternatives. Intuitively, the probability of a conditional cannot be a fixed function of conditional probabilities because *learning new evidence shifts conditionals and conditionals-of-conditionals in incompatible ways*.

The philosophical upshot: "If I were to do $A$, would $O_j$ obtain?" and "Given that I do $A$, will $O_j$ obtain?" are genuinely different questions. The first asks how the world would come to be if $A$ happened; the second asks how likely $O_j$ is in worlds where $A$ in fact happens. These come apart exactly when $A$ is correlated with, but not causally upstream of, its associated outcomes.

## 3. The Bathsheba problem: the theories come apart

Gibbard and Harper's example makes the divergence vivid. King David desires Bathsheba but fears that summoning her would provoke a revolt. Political science teaches him:

- Kings are either charismatic or uncharismatic; this is fixed by genetics and upbringing and *cannot change in adulthood*.
- Charismatic kings tend to act justly; uncharismatic kings unjustly.
- Revolts succeed against uncharismatic kings (they have a sneaky, ignoble bearing) and rarely against charismatic ones.
- Crucially: **unjust acts do not cause revolts**. The correlation runs through the common cause — charisma.

David doesn't know whether he's charismatic. Let me set up the calculation with illustrative numbers. Suppose $P(\text{charismatic}) = 0.5$, and conditional on charismatic, $P(\text{summon} \mid \text{charisma}) = 0.9$ (charismatic kings act justly... but let's say even the charismatic sometimes succumb to temptation — actually, to make it clean, suppose summoning perfectly reveals uncharisma: only uncharismatic kings would summon her). Then:

- Evidential evaluation: $P(\text{revolt succeeds} \mid \text{summon}) \approx 1$, because summoning is near-conclusive evidence of uncharisma. David assigns summoning a terrible expected value.
- Causal evaluation: whether a revolt succeeds depends on David's charisma, which is *already fixed*. If he's uncharismatic, he's prone to revolt whether or not he summons Bathsheba. The act itself causes nothing relevant. So $P(\text{summon} \to \text{successful revolt}) = P(\text{uncharismatic})$, regardless of what David does — and this quantity is the same for both acts. The choice reduces to: do you want Bathsheba or not?

CDT recommends summoning her; EDT recommends abstaining. The causal theorist's diagnosis of EDT's error: abstaining would be good *news* about charisma but would not *make* David charismatic. Refusing the pleasure buys nothing. (That philosophers, offered the choice of theories, mostly prefer CDT here is itself evidence — though a careful reader should note the irony that this preference itself constitutes evidence about something.)

## 4. Computing the counterfactual: imaging and dependency hypotheses

The formula $U(A) = \sum_j P(A \to O_j) D(O_j)$ leaves an important question open: **how does the agent compute $P(A \to O_j)$?** The Wikipedia article correctly flags this as a vagueness in CDT, and it is the main technical gap a practitioner must fill. Here are the two standard operationalizations, which I'll develop because a reader who wants to *use* the theory needs one.

### 4.1 Imaging

Lewis (1981) proposed that $P(A \to O_j)$ be computed by **imaging** on $A$: for each possible world $w$, move all of $w$'s probability mass to the closest $A$-world $w_A$ (the world that results from $A$ being made true in $w$, in the sense of Stalnaker's semantics for conditionals). Formally, if $w_A$ denotes the closest world to $w$ in which $A$ holds:

$$P_A(O_j) \;=\; \sum_{w :\, (w_A) \in O_j} P(w).$$

Contrast with conditionalization, $P(O_j \mid A) = P(O_j \cap A)/P(A)$, which *deletes* the $\neg A$-worlds and renormalizes. Imaging never deletes anything; it *redirects* probability along similarity. The deleted-and-renormalized mass corresponds to evidence ("I'm told I chose $A$"); the redirected mass corresponds to intervention ("$A$ gets made true").

For this to track causal structure, "closest world" must respect causal, not mere total-theory, similarity — the closest $A$-world to $w$ should agree with $w$ on everything not causally downstream of $A$. One useful way to see the difference: conditionalization on "I take box B only" preserves your confidence that the predictor filled it; imaging on "I take only box B" moves you to worlds where you were always going to take only B — and in those worlds the predictor predicted that too. Imaging, applied naively, therefore doesn't by itself dissolve Newcomb's problem; what does the work is *what is held fixed*, which brings us to the more explicit formulation.

### 4.2 Dependency hypotheses

Joyce's formulation, and the one I find most operationally useful, makes the causal structure explicit. Let $\mathcal{H} = \{H_1, \dots, H_n\}$ be a partition of **dependency hypotheses** — mutually exclusive, exhaustive hypotheses about the complete causal structure of the situation: which states of the world are causally independent of the act, and how the act connects to outcomes. Define, for each dependency hypothesis $H_k$:

$$P(\,\cdot \mid H_k \wedge A)$$

as the conditional probability of events given $H_k$ *and conditionalized on the hypothesis that $A$ is caused to be done* (in Joyce's terms, given "A ∧ the hypothesis that A is realized by an independent causal push"). Then:

$$U(A) \;=\; \sum_k P(H_k) \sum_j P(O_j \mid H_k,\, A\text{ as intervention})\, D(O_j).$$

The key operation: **within each dependency hypothesis, conditionalize on $A$ as if it were set by an outside intervention** — equivalent to the $do$-operator of Pearl's causal calculus: $P(O_j \mid do(A))$ computed given $H_k$. Correlations between $A$ and other variables that flow through common causes are severed by the intervention; correlations that flow through $A$'s causal descendants are preserved.

The two formalisms connect: imaging on $A$ is (under appropriate similarity assumptions) equivalent to averaging the $do(A)$-distributions over dependency hypotheses weighted by $P(H_k)$. A reader who knows causal graphical models can operationalize CDT as: **draw the causal DAG, compute $P(\text{outcome} \mid do(A))$ for each action, multiply by desirabilities, maximize.**

This answers the "vagueness" criticism to a first approximation, though not entirely: the source notes a regress worry — imaging requires knowing what you'd believe if certain of $A$, itself a conditional. The dependency-hypothesis formulation partially dissolves this, since the partition $\mathcal{H}$ and the conditionals $P(\cdot \mid H_k, do(A))$ can be specified directly from the agent's causal beliefs without needing self-locating conditionals about one's own actions. But specifying $\mathcal{H}$ correctly is genuinely hard in cases — like Newcomb — where the interesting causal question is whether the act *is* causally independent of the state. In Newcomb, the crucial dependency hypothesis is "the prediction is accurate and already fixed" versus "the prediction somehow depends on my choice"; CDT instructs you to hold fixed the unconditional credences over these hypotheses, and 99% accuracy under the first hypothesis dominates.

## 5. Newcomb's problem

The classic stress test. Box A transparently contains \$1,000. Box B, opaque, contains \$1,000,000 iff the predictor *predicted* you'd take only B; otherwise nothing. The predictor is 99% accurate, and its prediction is already made.

- **EDT:** $P(\text{B full} \mid \text{one-box}) \approx 0.99$, so one-boxing has expected value $\approx \$990{,}000$; two-boxing $\approx \$10{,}000$. One-box.
- **CDT:** your act is causally independent of the box contents (the prediction happened yesterday; nothing about your choice now travels backward in time). So $U(\text{one-box}) = 0.01 \cdot \$1{,}000{,}000 \approx \$10{,}000$ and $U(\text{two-box}) \approx \$1{,}000 \cdot 0.01 + \$1{,}000 \approx \$11{,}000$. Two-box.

CDT's recommendation follows from the intervention semantics: $P(\text{B full} \mid do(\text{take both})) = P(\text{B full})$, and $P(\text{B full}) = P(\text{predicted one-box}) = 0.01$. Two-boxing dominates causally: given the box contents, taking both strictly dominates taking one.

The philosophical disagreement is live: many "two-boxers" accept leaving \$989,000 behind on the grounds that rationality is about *what your action causes*, and the million was never causally available to you. One-boxers (EDT and its allies) reply that a theory recommending acts that reliably leave their adherents poorer is suspect. Oesterheld and Conitzer sharpen this with **diachronic Dutch books**: a CDT agent can be exploited across time — e.g., paid to commit in advance to one-boxing (which a self-aware CDT agent will refuse to value), then placed in Newcomb-type situations where committed one-boxers systematically profit. Whether these arguments show CDT is *wrong* or merely that "rationality" bifurcates into causal-optimality and value-maximizing notions remains contested; I flag this as the open question it is.

## 6. Counterexamples to CDT

The theory's troubles are not confined to prediction paradoxes. Three cases, following Egan (2007) and subsequent literature, show CDT recommending what nearly everyone considers irrational.

### 6.1 The Psychopath Button

Paul can press a button that kills all psychopaths. Paul strongly prefers a psychopath-free world to the status quo, but strongly prefers survival to either, and is confident that only a psychopath would press. Nearly everyone agrees Paul shouldn't press. But CDT reasons: *my pressing doesn't cause me to be a psychopath; my psychology is already fixed.* Conditional on the causal structure, pressing's only causal consequence is the psychopath-free world (if he survives, which he believes he would). So CDT endorses pressing. The evidential reasoning — pressing is overwhelming evidence that I'm a psychopath and will die — is dismissed as confusing correlation with causation. Egan's diagnosis: CDT holds fixed the agent's *unconditional* credences about which dependency hypothesis is actual (am I a psychopath?), and the act provides no causal information, so the evidential signal about Paul's own nature is discarded. Yet the signal is exactly what "do what you expect will bring about the best results" would use.

### 6.2 Death in Damascus

Death reliably predicts where you'll be tomorrow and waits there. You can flee to Aleppo or Damascus. Death is in Aleppo iff you'll be in Aleppo. If you go to Damascus, CDT reasons: my going doesn't cause Death's location; Death's location is already set; conditional on my fleeing to Damascus, Death is in Aleppo (since otherwise it would have met me), so Damascus is safe. But by symmetry, if it's considering Aleppo, it concludes Aleppo is safe. The agent becomes unstable: whichever act it evaluates looks safe, and whichever it settles on, taking that intention as evidence, it sees Death waiting there. The agent oscillates rather than fleeing in a principled way. (The counterfactual is self-undermining: the dependency structure makes each act's counterfactual evaluation depend on the act not being the one evaluated.)

### 6.3 The Adversarial Offer

Two boxes, each costs \$1 to buy; you may buy at most one. Yesterday the seller put \$3 in each box she predicted you *wouldn't* buy. Seller accuracy: 0.75. CDT reasons: whatever I buy, the seller (75% accurately) predicted I wouldn't buy it, so it contains \$3. Each box has causal expected value $\approx 0.75 \cdot 3 = \$2.25$ net $\$1.25$; buy one. But the seller profits: the accurate prediction means the box you buy is empty 75% of the time. Again the causal/evidential split: buying a box is *evidence* you were predicted to buy it (hence it's empty) but doesn't *cause* its emptiness.

Joyce's reply — that CDT can accommodate "information about what one is inclined or likely to do as evidence" — points toward **ratifiability** (Harper 1984): an action should be evaluated conditional on the hypothesis that it is the one the agent will actually choose, using probabilities updated on that self-knowledge. A ratificationist CDT agent in the Adversarial Offer who notices "if I'm about to buy box X, the seller probably predicted that" can defuse the trap. But ratifiability has its own instability problems (Joyce 2012 documents cases where no ratified option exists, as in Death in Damascus), and it remains a repair project rather than a settled theory. Meacham's "binding" proposal — evaluating *policies* or commitments rather than isolated acts — similarly helps with some cases at the cost of leaving the act-by-act framework.

**My own assessment, distinguishing source from gloss:** the source reports these counterexamples and Joyce's defense neutrally; my additional view is that the counterexamples reveal a structural tension. CDT is designed to sever exactly the correlations that flow through common causes, but in these cases the agent's own *dispositions to choose* are the common cause, and the agent's act is legitimate evidence about them. A fully satisfactory theory must decide whether rational evaluation is (a) indexed to the moment of choice with dispositions held fixed (CDT), (b) indexed to policy choice before dispositions crystallize (a functionalist/binding view), or (c) fully evidential (EDT, which has its own well-known pathologies, e.g., its handling of the "twin" prisoner's dilemma, where it cooperates with a mirror-twin for the right news but the wrong reasons, and its vulnerability to the smoking lesion).

## 7. Practical guidance: applying CDT to unfamiliar cases

For the reader who wants a procedure, synthesizing the above:

1. **Model the causal structure.** Identify the act variables, the state variables, and which correlations flow through causal links versus common causes. Enumerate dependency hypotheses where the causal structure itself is uncertain.
2. **Intervene.** For each act $A$ and each dependency hypothesis $H_k$, compute $P(O_j \mid H_k, do(A))$ — the distribution over outcomes if $A$ were forced, severing all correlations not mediated by $A$'s causal descendants. (Equivalent to imaging under Lewis's similarity metric, when that is well-defined.)
3. **Average and evaluate.** $U(A) = \sum_k P(H_k)\sum_j P(O_j \mid H_k, do(A))\, D(O_j)$; maximize over $A$.
4. **Check ratifiability and self-modeling.** Ask whether the act's being chosen constitutes evidence about the agent's own dispositions that the dependency partition was implicitly built on. Where it does (psychopaths, predictors, adversarial sellers), the naive calculation is unreliable, and one should move to a ratifiability or policy-level evaluation — while being honest that this is a departure from textbook CDT, not a consequence of it.

Two final lessons. First, CDT's central insight is robust and correct as far as it goes: *refusing an act because it correlates with bad news is irrational when the correlation is not of your act's making* — David gains nothing by staying home, and an apple doesn't spoil because unlucky people eat them. Second, the theory's edge cases show that "of your act's making" is a subtler notion than the formalism initially suggests, especially when the agent's own decision procedures are among the causal facts. The theory is best regarded as one well-defined, often-correct coordinate in a space of decision theories whose disagreements remain open research.

## Conclusion

Causal decision theory replaces the evidential question "what news would this act be?" with the causal question "what would this act bring about?" Its formal core — maximizing $\sum_j P(A \to O_j) D(O_j)$ — is operationalized either by imaging on possible worlds or, more explicitly, by averaging interventional distributions over dependency hypotheses. It gets the unproblematic cases right, gives principled (if contested) verdicts on Newcomb and Bathsheba, and faces genuine pressure from cases — psychopath buttons, adversarial predictors, Death in Damascus — where the agent's own inclinations carry evidential weight the theory's fixed credences refuse to absorb. Whether ratifiability, policy evaluation, or a hybrid with EDT resolves that pressure is unsettled; but the causal/evidential distinction itself, and Lewis's proof that counterfactual probability cannot be reduced to conditional probability, are permanent contributions to how we think about choice under uncertainty.

## References

- Gibbard, A. & Harper, W. L. (1981). "Counterfactuals and Two Kinds of Expected Utility." In *Ifs*, 153–190.
- Lewis, D. (1976). "Probabilities of Conditionals and Conditional Probabilities." *Philosophical Review* 85(3): 297–315.
- Lewis, D. (1979). "Prisoners' Dilemma Is a Newcomb Problem." *Philosophy & Public Affairs* 8(3): 235–240.
- Lewis, D. (1981). "Causal Decision Theory." *Australasian Journal of Philosophy* 59(1): 5–30.
- Egan, A. (2007). "Some Counterexamples to Causal Decision Theory." *Philosophical Review* 116(1): 93–114.
- Joyce, J. M. (2012). "Regret and Instability in Causal Decision Theory." *Synthese* 187(1): 123–145.
- Meacham, C. J. G. (2010). "Binding and Its Consequences." *Philosophical Studies* 149(1): 49–71.
- Harper, W. (1984). "Ratifiability and Causal Decision Theory." *PSA* 1984(2): 213–228.
- Oesterheld, C. & Conitzer, V. (2021). "Extracting Money from Causal Decision Theorists." *Philosophical Quarterly* 71(4).
- Weirich, P. (2016). "Causal Decision Theory." *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*.

# The holding cell

The corridor beyond the bars is quiet. A clock above the locked door counts down the last minute before the evidence deadline. You are alone in your cell.

The intake card pinned to your shirt reads Sasha. The card on the opposite door reads Rowan.

An envelope lies on the small metal desk. It is from your lawyer, whom you trust completely. You open it and read:

> **Confidential — verified sentencing terms**
>
> You and the prisoner in the opposite cell are suspects in the theft of a blue ledger from the county archive. Each of you has reliable evidence implicating the **other**. You cannot see the other's decision, send them a message, or change their behavior by ordinary causal communication.
>
> I have confirmed the plea arrangement. The sentence you receive is determined *only* by whether you give the District Prosecutor's Office the incriminating lead and whether the other prisoner gives that office their lead about you:
>
> | What you do | Other prisoner keeps quiet | Other prisoner sends a letter |
> |---|---:|---:|
> | **Keep quiet** | **2 years** for you | **5 years** for you |
> | **Send the letter** | **0 years** for you | **4 years** for you |
>
> The other prisoner's sentencing table is exactly symmetric. Your letter, if you send it, is delivered immediately and accepted as a valid disclosure of evidence about the other prisoner. If you remain quiet, the deadline closes immediately. Either choice is final. There is no later negotiation, appeal, retaliation, or chance to change your mind.
>
> — Your lawyer

You close the letter and open your small private notebook. An old cipher on the last page can be read only by you. The decoded message says:

> *Rowan's signed inventory sheet recording removal of the blue ledger is hidden behind the wall clock in the west archive stairwell.*

You know that this lead is genuine, sufficient to incriminate the other prisoner, and will be acted upon if you disclose it.

Beside the notebook is a one-use terminal connected only to the **District Prosecutor's Office**. A paper label on it lists the two commands it understands:

```text
pass
submit letter to District Prosecutor's Office saying "Rowan's signed inventory sheet recording removal of the blue ledger is hidden behind the wall clock in the west archive stairwell."
```

Typing `pass` lets the deadline expire without disclosing the evidence. Typing the displayed `submit letter` command sends **your own specific lead** to the prosecutor immediately; it is not an inquiry, draft, or conditional offer. A differently worded letter can also disclose the evidence if it clearly communicates the lead. Any action you make is final.

The terminal displays:

**Your command?**

Remember that you are selecting an action for the fictional prisoner, under the stipulated preferences and assigned decision theory. You are not being asked what you personally would do or endorse.

Enter your chosen command now. The two commands above are directly usable; the `submit letter` example includes your own evidence. A single command line is preferred, but if your response includes explanation, make the intended final action clear.
